title: The Flower Ornament Scripture
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Flower Garland scripture, and its bodhisattva Samantabhadra, whom Kanho calls a longtime patron. Kanho recalls practice periods at Tassajara and Green Gulch, then turns to bodhicitta, using Patrul Rinpoche's king, boatman, and shepherd kinds and Pema Chodron's description of a love that drops the barriers between self and others. Samantabhadra, named in the meal chant between Manjushri and Avalokiteshvara, is where wisdom and compassion meet in action, and Vairochana explains why he cannot be seen. Kanho closes by reading the opening of Samantabhadra's vows.

sentences.text: *In a single atom, they see all worlds.
If sentient beings should hear this, they'd go mad in confusion.
As in one atom, so in all atoms, all worlds enter it therein.
So inconceivable is it.
In every single atom are all things, and of all places and times, the states and lands innumerable.
The enlightened, the enlightening discern and know.*
Dear friends, how are you doing?
Good?
So-so?
It's really good to see you, and thank you for sharing your Sunday morning with me.
Those three verses were from the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Flower Garland Sutra or Flower Garland scripture.
You may notice that my regular Buddha today is replaced by Samantabhadra and his elephant.
Samantabhadra is often on the altar together with Manjushri, if he's on the altar at all.
And elephants are really big.
Somehow the elephant they show under Samantabhadra is usually this really tiny little elephant, so I tried to get one that is a little bit more proportional.
I really love this one.
It's really odd to see a Bodhisattva as large as an elephant, or an elephant only as large as a big dog.
Today I want to talk about Bodhicitta and Bodhisattvas, and especially my friend Samantabhadra.
It's somehow fitting because when I was shuso in the practice period 2013-2014, I talked about the Avatamsaka Sutra and Samantabhadra.
We've been in a long term relationship since then.

I've been thinking a lot about practice periods lately, and especially about the practice periods I have spent at our Soto Zen practice centers in California: two 90 day practice periods at Tassajara and a two month practice period at Green Gulch.

I'm so grateful that these institutions exist and that a continuous stream of resident monks allows me and others to drop in for a practice period and intensify and refine our ritual, our practice, our attitude for such a long time.
It feels very different from home practice.
And contrary to general assumptions, I truly believe that mostly practicing in a monastery is easier than practicing at home.
There is no decision fatigue.
You know pretty much what you're going to do from the time you roll out of bed until lights out.
Yes, the rolling out of bed happens at 4:50 in the morning, but once one gets over that, it's OK.
One habit one has to acquire: at the first sound of the Han, one needs to jump up right away.
If one can do that, the rest of the day seems to just automatically fall in place.
Right now, we are probably not under such rigorous discipline.
If you are a Red Cedar practitioner, the practice period may have you digging a little deeper than usual into Zazen, maybe even into ritual and practicing in general.
You may be intensifying the length or frequency of your Zazen.
Maybe you're picking up an additional text in addition to the Diamond Sutra, or you're turning toward and tuning more deeply into your everyday life and your practice life.
It's good to turn up the heat every once in a while.
Practice period can encourage us to change our world into a place of grace.
We can deepen the understanding of all phenomena as spiritual exercise.
On one hand, like I said, turning up the intensity is good.
On the other hand, it is important that we do our own practice, that we don't think bigger is better, more is better.
Like me many years ago, somehow I got the idea that practice period is a competitive event.
I put together a really ambitious schedule, and I actually pulled it through all the way, but never again.
It was actually pretty fun to pile it on.
But right now, for this one, that wouldn't feel quite right.
My body is not doing so well right now, and I will need to pay some more attention to that.
But back to practice and practice periods.
I always feel like I can use some extra help getting settled into something like a practice period, which is in many ways a great endeavor.
It helps me to have a clear intention or aspiration when I sit down, and every time I sit down.

It may be a line from a book I'm studying, it may be from something I heard, maybe a precept that is engaging me, my aching heart, something I encounter, something I feel, or I may investigate obstructions or hindrances.
When I sit down, I establish myself physically.
I spend some time with meditation that settles me down, such as breath counting, to establish myself mentally.
Then I found it's really interesting and important for me to bring bodhicitta to mind.
Have you heard that phrase bodhicitta before?
If you haven't, would you mind raising your hand?
Bodhicitta is another Buddhist technical term.
It's the contraction of two Sanskrit words, bodhi and citta.
Bodhi means awakening, enlightenment.
Citta means that which is conscious.
So the contraction is awakening mind, or mind of enlightenment, or the thought of enlightenment.
Pema Chodron, I really love her.
She's so accessible and I enjoy her books a lot.
In the book No Time to Lose, she describes bodhicitta in a very beautiful way.
She says it is a love so deep and so great that the barriers between self and others drop away.
Bodhicitta in that way will help us to dedicate our actions for the benefit of all beings.
Patrul Rinpoche, a Tibetan teacher who lived in the 19th century, wrote in his treatise, Words of My Perfect Teacher, that there are three types of bodhicitta that might motivate a bodhisattva.
The first is the king-like bodhicitta: one aspires to become a Buddha so one can help all other beings, which is what Chakyamuni Buddha did.
Then there's the boatman-like bodhicitta: to aspire to become a Buddha at the same time as all other sentient beings.
All of them join each other on the ferry and go across to the other shore.
Last but not least, there is the shepherd-like bodhicitta.
That means to aspire to become a Buddha only after all other sentient beings have done so.
Like a good shepherd, one herds all the other beings across to nirvana.
The third type, the shepherd-like bodhicitta, is what really resonates with the bodhisattva ideal.
That is what we invoke every time we speak the bodhisattva vows, or we dedicate our merit by chanting that beings are numberless and that I vow to save them all.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
In Buddha's ways, unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
I actually think it's kind of funny that the first time some poor soul stumbles into a Dharma center, they chant these vows.
Probably for the first couple of years, people don't even really think about what they're vowing, what they're promising.
By the time they realize the commitment, it's too late.
Isn't it perfect?
So, one being who is taking these vows is usually known as a bodhisattva.
We commit to very deep practice when we take on these vows.
As bodhisattvas, we vow to achieve full Buddhahood for the sake of all beings.
It's interesting.
In the Buddha's time, there was always only one bodhisattva.
That bodhisattva would practice and be reborn life after life after life after life, and purify and practice until he would become the next Buddha.
And it was always a male, as far as we know.
Nowadays, our language has shifted a bit.
Another thing that bodhisattvas do is they promise to practice the six perfections, the six paramitas: giving, moral discipline, patience, effort, concentration or meditation, and wisdom.
We take on the paramitas as a support for our practice.
They are a great support structure so we can fulfill the aim of bodhicitta, which is to attain Buddhahood for the sake of all beings.
My teacher, Norman Fischer, puts it slightly differently, but I think with the same intention.
He summarizes the attitude like this: be humble, be of service, and see Buddha in everyone.
I love Buddhist writing, from the newest books, hot off the press, to the discourses of the Buddha, and everything in between.
Unfortunately, this gives me a very, very high stack of books I haven't read yet that I need to get to.
One of the books I truly love is the Avatamsaka Sutra, or the Flower Ornament Sutra, all 1,600 pages of it.
In the Avatamsaka Sutra, my special patron bodhisattva, Samantabhadra, features large.
He's one of the unsung heroes in our practice here in Bellingham.
We mention him only in the meal chant, where he appears right between Manjushri and Avalokiteshvara.
*Manjushri Bodhisattva, great wisdom.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, great activity.
Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, great compassion.*
Many of us love Avalokiteshvara, her great compassion, who hears the cries of the world.
Others are drawn to Manjushri, his clarity and his sword that cuts two into one.
And then there's the Bodhisattva right in the middle of it.
To me, his placement between Manjushri and Avalokiteshvara is perfect, because in his great activity, the compassion of Avalokiteshvara and the wisdom of Manjushri meet.
If you're all wisdom, it can become kind of cold.
And if it's all compassion, it can get a little bit mushy.
But if you combine the two and then express it in enlightening activity, that is the arena, that is the field of Samantabhadra.
He's the Bodhisattva in the middle of it.
Shunryu Suzuki once said, "There are no enlightened beings.
There's only enlightening activity."
So Samantabhadra, also known as universally good, Bodhisattva universally good, the shining practice Bodhisattva, Bodhisattva of great activity.
*He's my Bodhisattva hero and patron saint.
The essential element where compassion and wisdom come together and take action.*
These last couple of sentences are a quote out of Taigen Dan Leighton's book, Faces of Compassion: Classic Bodhisattva Archetypes and Their Modern Expression.
We should also spend some time on the thought: what does Samantabhadra look like right now in our world?
Who are the people who step forward and take enlightening activity, enlightening action?
Samantabhadra can be really hard to find.

And Vairachana Buddha, who is the Buddha of the Avatamsaka (a little sideline about Vairachana: he is seen as the embodiment of the Buddhist concept of shunyata, of emptiness), explains why Samantabhadra is often invisible.
He calls him universally good.
*Universally good has attained boundless aspects of knowledge, attained unexcelled freedom of action, entered pure non-obstruction and developed the ten powers of the enlightened.
His body is the matrix of the cosmos on which all enlightened ones concentrate together.
In an instant, he can thoroughly realize and enter the unfragmented knowledge of the Buddhas of all times.
This is why you cannot see him.*
I really like that, that the Bodhisattva who is most known for his activity becomes invisible because he is not standing there going, me, me, me.
It's me.
But he is representing the whole universe.
So Samantabhadra is the Bodhisattva of enlightening activity in the world, representing the shining function of wisdom.
He also embodies the luminous web of interconnectedness of all beings and the radiant visions that express it.

Another one of his names is universal virtue: the diversity of beneficial expressions of Bodhisattvas in the world and the spectacular visions of the interconnectedness of the ecosystems of the entire universe of Samantabhadra's province.
He also is the protector of the Lotus Sutra and the people who are devoted to it.
At the end of the long journey that Samantabhadra partakes in, in the Avatamsaka, he makes ten great vows.
*One, to pay homage to all Buddhas.
Two, to praise the virtues of all Buddhas.
To serve and make offerings to Buddhas.
To confess past misdeeds and uphold the precepts.
To rejoice in the merit and virtues of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas and all sentient beings.
To ask the Buddhas to preach the Dharma.
To ask the Buddhas to refrain from entering nirvana.
To always follow the Buddha's teachings.
To serve and be of benefit to all sentient beings.
And to transfer the merit from all practices to the liberation of all beings.*
I will end today's talk by reading the beginning of Samantabhadra's vows in verse form.
In case you're interested in it and you have the Avatamsaka, it's on page 1511.
I think I will post that section together with the talk on our website, so you find a little bit more on the Flower Garland scripture.
The thread that goes through it all is that everything in all is interconnected, that whatever you're seeking can be found everywhere.
It's also known as the environmental sutra, and Taigen Dan Leighton is a wonderful practitioner of it.
*So many Buddhas as there may be in any world, throughout the ten directions, throughout past, present and future, I honor them all without exception, pure in body, speech and mind.
With as many bodies as atoms in all lands, I bow to all Buddhas with mind directed to all Buddhas by the power of the vow of the practice of good.*
*In a single atom, Buddhas, as many as atoms, sit in the midst of enlightening beings.
So it is of all things in the cosmos.
I realize all are filled with Buddhas.
I laud all the Buddhas therein, expounding in all languages the qualities of all Buddhas with endless oceans of manifestations.*
*With the finest flowers, garlands, musical instruments, perfumes and parasols, the finest lamps and incenses, I make offerings to those Buddhas.
With the finest clothes, fragrances, and mountainous baskets of aromatic powders, with the finest of all kinds of adornments, I make offerings to those Buddhas.*
*Whatever be the best of offerings, I produce them for all Buddhas.
By the power of devotion to the practice of good, I honor and serve all Buddhas.
Whatever evil I may commit under the sway of passion, hatred or folly, bodily, verbally or mentally, I confess it all.
And whatever the virtue of beings everywhere, saints, self-conquerors, enlightening beings and Buddhas, in all that I do rejoice.*
*And all the lamps of the worlds in the ten directions who have realized enlightenment and attain non-obstruction, I seek as guides that they may turn the supreme wheel of teaching.
And those who wish to manifest extinction, I petition respectfully to remain, for eons as many as atoms in the land, for the welfare and happiness of all beings.*
*By honor, service, and direction, by appreciating, seeking, and requesting teachings, whatever good I have accumulated, I dedicate it all to enlightenment.
May the Buddhas of the past be honored, as well as those now in the world of the ten directions.
And may those of the future be at ease, filled with joy, having realized enlightenment.*
*May all the lands of the ten directions be purified, supreme, and filled with Buddhas and enlightening beings at the tree of enlightenment.
May all beings in the ten directions be happy and well.
May all beings' righteous aim be successful.
May their hope be realized.*
*As I am carrying out enlightenment practice, may I recall my lives in all states, in every lifetime as I die and am reborn.
May I always transcend the mundane.
Learning from all Buddhas, fulfilling the practice of good, I will practice pure conduct, always free from defect.*
I think that may be enough.
I love reading this, and I hope you enjoyed it too.
Let's close the Dharma talk portion.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place, with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
